svg.text: xmin is the xid that wrote the version. xmax is the xid that deleted or replaced it

xid 500 wrote both rows and committed. 56 bytes left on the page
UPDATE wrote a second version of row 1 and set xmax on the first. Page full
COMMIT changed nothing on this page. It marked 502 committed in the clog
two live versions, one dead. Every reader steps over it until VACUUM
VACUUM removed the dead version. 48 bytes free
the INSERT reused the 48 bytes. The table did not grow
DELETE marked Mike's row dead. Its bytes are still taken
VACUUM removed Mike's row. 48 bytes free

free space map (FSM), one entry per page
page 0: 48 bytes free. Too small for any row that comes in

SELECT again. Three rows, one of them on a new page
SELECT again. Still Smith. 502 is in flight, its version is invisible
SELECT again. Smith-Rivera. New statement, new snapshot
SELECT again. Two rows. 505 committed, Mike is gone
SELECT again. Three rows, one of them on a new page

64 bytes. Page 0 has 48 free, so the table grows a page
in flight: holds xid 502 and a connection
no lock on the table, readers and writers carry on
the FSM pointed at page 0, so Susie took the freed space
DELETE writes nothing new. It sets xmax, and the row is dead
64 bytes. Page 0 has 48 free, so the table grows a page
12. A row that does not fit
dead versions become free bytes. A row that fits reuses them; a row that does not grows the table and leaves the gap behind
xid 500 bulk-loads the table in one transaction and commits. The page is otherwise full
501 reads. Its snapshot is everything committed before the statement started
502 updates row 1. Postgres never overwrites: a new version is written, and the old one gets xmax = 502
501 reads again and still sees Smith. 502 has not committed, so its version is invisible to everyone else
502 commits. The page does not change; the commit log now says 502 is committed
501's next statement takes a new snapshot and sees Smith-Rivera (READ COMMITTED, the default)
the old version is dead. It stays on the page until VACUUM, and every reader steps over it until then
VACUUM compacts the page, frees the dead version's 48 bytes, and records them in the free space map
504 inserts Susie Rivera, 48 bytes after padding. The FSM points at page 0, so she takes the freed space
505 deletes Mike. DELETE writes nothing; it sets xmax, and once 505 commits the version is dead
VACUUM frees Mike's 48 bytes and the FSM records page 0 again
506 inserts a 64-byte row. 48 is not enough, so the table grows a page. The 48 bytes on page 0 stay empty: bloat
